title: The White Sneakers
teaser: Adham saved for a year to buy them. On the first day, it rained.
paragraphs: Adham is seventeen and loves sneakers. He watches sneaker videos every night and knows every new model. There is one pair he wants more than anything: white leather sneakers with a small blue logo. They are very expensive.
For a whole year, Adham saves money. He works at his uncle’s shop on weekends. He does not buy snacks at school. He puts every pound in a box under his bed.
Finally, he has enough. He goes to the mall with his best friend, Yassin, and buys them. He holds the box like it is a treasure. The next morning, he wears them to school. They are perfectly white.
Then, in the afternoon, something very unusual happens in Cairo: it rains. Heavily. The street outside the school becomes a river of mud. Adham looks at his sneakers and almost cries.

Yassin laughs, takes off his own shoes and gives Adham a plastic bag. “Put them in this,” he says. They walk home barefoot in the rain, laughing like crazy. At home, Adham cleans the sneakers carefully. They are white again. But now, his favourite memory is not the shoes. It is the walk home.

title: The Real Cost of a Cheap T-shirt
teaser: Fast fashion made clothes cheap. Somebody else pays the difference.
paragraphs: Fast fashion is a business model in which brands design, produce and sell clothes very quickly and cheaply, copying trends from catwalks and social media within weeks. Some companies release new items almost every day, encouraging customers to buy often and wear things only a few times.

Low prices are possible for several reasons. Clothes are made in huge quantities, often in countries where wages are low. Cheap synthetic materials such as polyester replace more expensive natural fibres. And speed is everything: shipping fast, selling fast and replacing what does not sell.

The environmental cost is significant. The fashion industry uses enormous amounts of water, especially for cotton and dyeing. Synthetic fabrics release tiny plastic fibres when washed, which end up in rivers and oceans. Many clothes are thrown away after short use, and only a small percentage is recycled into new clothing.

There is also a human cost. Investigations have revealed unsafe factories, very long working hours and wages too low to live on. In 2013, the collapse of a garment factory building in Bangladesh killed more than a thousand workers and led to new safety agreements.

Consumers can make a difference in small ways: buying fewer but better-quality clothes, repairing them, swapping with friends, and buying second-hand. Egypt has a long tradition of tailors and wekalat markets, where clothes get a second life.

made by people, not natural

title: Twelve Products
teaser: Jana copied a ten-step routine from the internet. Her skin was not happy.
paragraphs: Jana is nineteen. She watches beauty videos every day. One influencer has a twelve-step skincare routine: cleanser, toner, three serums, two creams, a mask and more. Her skin looks perfect. Jana wants the same skin.
She spends all her birthday money on the twelve products. Every night, she uses all of them. She feels very grown-up and very pretty.
After two weeks, her face is red and itchy. She has small spots on her cheeks. She tries more products to fix it, but it gets worse. She is afraid to go to university.

Her aunt takes her to a dermatologist. The doctor looks at the long list of products and smiles kindly. “Your skin is not broken,” she says. “It is tired. Too many strong products at the same time.” She tells Jana to stop everything for two weeks except a gentle cleanser, a simple moisturiser and sunscreen in the morning.

Slowly, Jana’s skin calms down. She learns that an influencer’s skin depends on many things: genes, lighting, filters and even sponsorships. Now Jana has a three-step routine. She still watches beauty videos, but she asks a new question: is this right for my skin?

title: What Does SPF 50 Actually Mean?
teaser: It is not about hours in the sun. Here is what the number really tells you.
paragraphs: Dermatologists often say that the most effective skincare product is not an expensive serum but sunscreen. Sunlight contains ultraviolet radiation, which damages skin cells. Over time, this causes sunburn, dark spots, wrinkles and, more seriously, skin cancer.

There are two main types of UV rays that reach us. UVB rays mainly cause sunburn. UVA rays go deeper into the skin and are strongly linked to ageing; they can even pass through windows. A good sunscreen protects against both, which is why many labels say “broad spectrum”.

SPF, or sun protection factor, measures protection against UVB. SPF 30 blocks about 97 percent of UVB rays, and SPF 50 about 98 percent. So the difference between 30 and 50 is smaller than most people think. What matters more is how you use it.

In laboratory tests, sunscreen is applied in a thick layer. Most people use only a quarter to half of that amount, so they get much less protection than the label promises. Sunscreen also wears off with sweat, water and touching your face, so it should be reapplied about every two hours outdoors.

Even people with darker skin, which has more natural protection, can be damaged by UV radiation. In a sunny country like Egypt, sunscreen every morning, along with shade and hats at midday, is one of the simplest health habits there is.

targets.en: energy that travels as waves or particles
a line on the skin, usually from age
the process of getting older
information printed on a product
to put a cream or liquid on a surface

questions.q: Which UV rays mainly cause sunburn?

questions.ar: ليه أغلب الناس بياخدوا حماية أقل؟

recap: Sunscreen protects against UVB (burns) and UVA (ageing); SPF 30 blocks about 97% of UVB, but most people apply too little and should reapply every two hours.

title: The Last Cinema in Town
teaser: The old cinema was closing. Mazen had one idea to save it.
paragraphs: In Mazen’s small town in the Delta, there is an old cinema called Cinema Al-Nour. It is ninety years old. Mazen’s grandfather watched his first film there. But now, almost nobody comes. People watch films on their phones. The owner, Am Gamal, is going to close it.

Mazen is twenty and studies film at university in Cairo. When he hears the news, he goes home for the weekend. He sits in the empty cinema with Am Gamal. The seats are old, but the big screen is still beautiful.

Mazen has an idea. “What if we make it a special place again?” he says. “Not only films. Events.” They plan a classic film night with old Egyptian black-and-white films, a short-film night for young filmmakers, and a Friday morning cartoon show for children.

Mazen posts photos of the old cinema online. People share their memories: “My parents met there!” “I saw my first film there!” On the first classic film night, the cinema is full. Old people come with their grandchildren.

Cinema Al-Nour does not become rich. But it stays open. Every month, Mazen comes back to help. On the wall in the lobby, there is now a photo of his grandfather as a young man, standing in front of the same door.

title: How Film Music Tells You What to Feel
teaser: Turn off the sound in a horror scene. Suddenly, it is not scary.
paragraphs: Try a simple experiment: watch a frightening scene from a horror film with the sound off. Often, it becomes surprisingly ordinary. Music and sound design do a huge part of the emotional work in films, frequently without the audience noticing.

Composers use a set of tools to shape our feelings. Low, slow notes can create a sense of danger or sadness, while high, fast strings can produce tension or excitement. Silence is powerful too: removing the music just before a shock makes the moment more intense.

Many films use a leitmotif, a short musical theme connected to a character, place or idea. When we hear it, we immediately think of that character, even if they are not on screen. Composers can change the leitmotif, making it slower, sadder or more heroic, to show how a character develops through the story.

Music can also tell us something the images do not. A cheerful song over a violent scene creates an uncomfortable contrast. A sad melody during a happy wedding can warn the audience that something bad is coming.

Some of the most memorable film themes use only a few notes. Their simplicity makes them easy to recognise and remember. Next time you watch a film, pay attention to the music for a few minutes. You may discover that you were being guided all along.

to influence how something develops
a main musical idea or tune

a clear difference between two things

title: No Spoilers, Please
teaser: The final episode was tonight. Hossam had to avoid everyone until then.
paragraphs: Hossam loves a crime series. He has watched every episode for three years. Tonight at nine, the final episode comes out. But Hossam works until eight, and all his friends will watch it at nine. He is very afraid of spoilers.
At work, he does not open social media. When his colleague starts to say, “Did you see the trailer for the last…”, Hossam puts his fingers in his ears and runs to the kitchen. Everyone laughs.
On the metro home, he sees a man watching the series on his phone. Did it come out early? Hossam closes his eyes and counts to one hundred. A woman looks at him strangely.
At home, his little sister Habiba is waiting at the door with a big smile. “I know what happens,” she sings. “I know who the killer is!” Hossam runs into his room and locks the door.

At nine o’clock, he watches the episode alone, with popcorn and no phone. The ending is a huge surprise. When it finishes, he opens the door. Habiba is still there. “I didn’t really know,” she says. “But your face was funny.”

title: The Cliffhanger: Why You Click Next Episode
teaser: Writers leave you hanging on purpose. Here is the science behind it.
paragraphs: An episode ends just as a character opens a door, receives a shocking phone call or is about to reveal a secret. The screen goes black. On a streaming platform, the next episode starts in five seconds, and you let it play. This is the cliffhanger, one of the oldest tricks in storytelling.

The name may come from nineteenth-century serial novels, published in parts in magazines. In one famous instalment, a character is left literally hanging from a cliff, and readers had to buy the next issue to find out what happened. Long before that, the storyteller of One Thousand and One Nights, Shahrazad, survived by stopping each story at the most exciting moment.

Psychologists link the power of cliffhangers to the Zeigarnik effect: people tend to remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones. An open question creates mental tension that the brain wants to resolve. The story stays in your head until you know the answer.

Writers plan cliffhangers carefully. A strong one raises a question that matters to the characters the audience cares about. A weak or fake one, where the danger is easily explained away in the next episode, can make viewers feel cheated.

Streaming services use this effect with autoplay, starting the next episode automatically. That is why it is so easy to watch a whole season in one weekend. Knowing the trick won’t make it disappear, but it can help you decide to stop, perhaps at the start of an episode instead of the end.

title: Drawing Every Day
teaser: Yara’s first anime drawing was terrible. She kept every single one.
paragraphs: Yara is fourteen and loves anime. She watches it after school and reads manga on her tablet. She wants to draw her own characters, with big eyes, wild hair and strong emotions.

Her first drawing is terrible. The eyes are different sizes, and the hands look like potatoes. Her brother laughs. Yara is angry and wants to throw the paper away. But her art teacher, Miss Nermeen, says, “Keep it. Write the date on it. And draw one more tomorrow.”

So Yara draws every day. Some days, she draws for an hour. Some days, she is tired and draws for only five minutes. She watches free tutorials about faces, hands and clothes. She practises drawing people on the bus.

After one year, she has 365 drawings in a big folder. She puts her first drawing next to her latest one. She cannot believe it. The new character is full of life, with beautiful eyes and perfect hands. Even her brother is impressed.

Yara starts to post her drawings online. Her favourite comment is from a girl in Morocco who writes, “Your drawings make me want to start.” Yara replies with a photo of her very first, terrible drawing. “Start here,” she writes.

title: How a Single Episode of Anime Is Made
teaser: Twenty-four minutes of animation can take months and hundreds of people.
paragraphs: A typical TV anime episode lasts about twenty-four minutes, but making it can involve hundreds of people and several months of work. The process follows a series of stages, each building on the last.

It begins with the script and the storyboard. The storyboard is like a comic version of the episode: rough drawings showing each shot, the camera angle, the characters’ movements and the timing. The director uses it to plan exactly how the episode will look.

Next come the key animators. They draw the most important frames of each movement, such as the beginning and end of a punch or a turn of the head. Then in-between animators draw the frames in between, creating smooth motion. To save time and money, many anime scenes use fewer drawings per second than Western cartoons, holding some frames for longer, which gives anime its distinctive style.

The drawings are scanned or drawn digitally, coloured and combined with painted backgrounds. A compositing team adds lighting, shadows and special effects. Finally, voice actors record the dialogue, and composers and sound designers add music and effects.

The industry is famous for beautiful results but also for difficult working conditions. Many animators work long hours for low pay, especially early in their careers. In recent years, some studios have improved conditions, and fans increasingly support creators by watching through official services.

title: A Logo for Uncle Saber
teaser: Uncle Saber’s koshary shop had no sign. Laila had a pencil and an idea.
paragraphs: Laila is a design student in Cairo. Near her university, there is a small koshary shop owned by Uncle Saber. The food is delicious, but the shop has no sign. Many students walk past it and do not know what it is.
One day, Laila asks Uncle Saber, “Can I design a logo and a sign for you? For free. It is practice for me.” Uncle Saber laughs. “A logo? For koshary?” But he says yes.

Laila starts with questions. What makes the shop special? Uncle Saber says, “My crispy onions. My mother’s recipe.” Laila draws twenty ideas in her sketchbook: bowls, onions, smiling faces. Most of them are bad. She keeps going.

Finally, she has an idea. She draws a simple bowl of koshary, and the crispy onions on top form the shape of a smile. She uses two colours: warm orange and dark brown. She writes the name in big, friendly Arabic letters: “Koshary Saber”.

A carpenter makes the sign, and they put it above the door. Students start to notice the shop and take photos of the smiling bowl. Uncle Saber orders T-shirts with the logo for his workers. He tells everyone, “My designer is a genius.” Laila puts the logo first in her portfolio.

title: Why Designers Choose Colours So Carefully
teaser: Red for sales, blue for banks — is there really a colour code?
paragraphs: Look at the logos of fast-food chains, banks and tech companies, and you may notice patterns. Many fast-food brands use red and yellow; many banks prefer blue. These choices are rarely random. Designers use colour to create feelings, guide attention and make information easier to understand.

Colours have associations, though they depend partly on culture. In many places, red suggests energy, urgency and appetite, which is why it appears in sales signs and restaurants. Blue is often linked with calm and trust, which suits banks and health apps. Green is associated with nature and growth. However, white is the colour of weddings in some cultures and of mourning in others, so global brands must be careful.

Contrast is just as important as colour. Text must stand out clearly from its background to be readable, especially for people with weak eyesight. Accessibility guidelines recommend a minimum contrast ratio between text and background, and good designers check this with tools.

Designers also consider colour blindness. Around one in twelve men has some form of it, most commonly difficulty telling red from green. That is why important information, like an error message, should not depend on colour alone; an icon or a word should support it.

Finally, fewer colours usually look more professional. Many designers follow a simple rule: one main colour, one or two supporting colours, and plenty of neutral space. Restraint makes the important things stand out.

title: A Film Made With a Phone
teaser: No money, no camera, no actors. Two weeks until the festival deadline.
paragraphs: Abdelrahman is nineteen and wants to be a film director. He finds a short-film competition online. The deadline is in two weeks. The problem: he has no camera, no money and no actors.
He has a phone, a cheap microphone and a story. It is about an old man who sells newspapers in Downtown Cairo, and a boy who helps him every morning. It is a simple story about friendship.

His actors are his own grandfather and his little cousin, Hamza. Grandpa is nervous in front of the camera. He looks at the phone and forgets his words. So Abdelrahman changes his plan. He lets Grandpa talk naturally and films him without telling him when the recording starts.

They film early in the morning, when the light is soft and the streets are quiet. Abdelrahman learns a lot: keep the phone steady, record clean sound, and film each scene from different angles. He edits everything at night on a free app.

He sends the film one hour before the deadline. A month later, he gets an email: his film is selected for the festival. At the screening, Grandpa sees himself on the big screen and holds Abdelrahman’s hand very tightly.

title: Composition: Where to Put Things in the Frame
teaser: The rule of thirds, leading lines, and when to break the rules.
paragraphs: Two people can photograph the same scene with the same phone and get very different results. Often, the difference is not the camera but composition: how the elements are arranged inside the frame.

The best-known guideline is the rule of thirds. Imagine dividing the frame into nine equal parts with two horizontal and two vertical lines. Placing an important subject, such as a person’s eyes or the horizon, along these lines or at the points where they cross usually creates a more balanced and interesting image than putting everything in the exact centre. Most phone cameras can show this grid on the screen.

Leading lines are another tool. Roads, rivers, railings and shadows can guide the viewer’s eye towards the subject. Framing is similar: shooting through a doorway, a window or between trees creates a natural frame within the frame and adds depth.

In video, composition also involves movement. Filmmakers leave “looking room” in front of a character’s face in the direction they are looking, and “lead room” in the direction they are moving. Without this space, the image can feel uncomfortable, as if the character is about to hit the edge of the screen.

These are guidelines, not laws. A perfectly centred, symmetrical shot can be powerful, especially with buildings or to create a feeling of order. The aim is to understand the rules well enough to break them on purpose.
